lessons.title: The flags
lessons.objective: Match every flag to its meaning and consequence in a race.

payload.prompt: Match the flag to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Signals the start or restart of full-speed racing.
Slows the field for an incident or debris.
Stops the race completely for safety.
Shows one lap remaining.
Ends the race; the first car wins.
Orders a driver to pit for a penalty.

distractorDefinitions: Means the leader is two laps ahead.
Signals a mandatory pit stop for everyone.

explanation.summary: Flags signal changes in race status: go, slow, stop, warning, finish, and penalty.

payload.prompt: Which flag ends the race?

image.alt: Four racing flags in a row: solid green, solid yellow, checkered black-and-white, and solid white.

options.text: Green
Yellow
Checkered
White

cues: Look for the pattern, not the color.

explanation.correct: Right. The checkered pattern is unmistakable. First car across after the checker wins it.
explanation.incorrect: The checkered flag ends the race. The winning car crosses the line and the moment is history.

payload.prompt: When the yellow flag waves, what happens next?

options.text: All cars slow and line up behind the pace car.
Drivers pit immediately for fresh tires.
The race is finished and rescheduled.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The pace car leads the field while everyone slows and bunches up.
explanation.incorrect: When yellow waves, the pace car takes the lead and all cars slow. Teams choose whether to pit once pit road opens, and the race stays slow until green comes back.

payload.prompt: If a red flag is thrown with 10 laps to go, can the race still finish?

scene.alt: Scenario: a big wreck with 10 laps to go, red flag thrown, cars stopped while crews repair the barrier.

choices.label: Yes, the race resumes after repairs.
No, red flags always end the race.

explanation.correct: Right. Red flags pause the race, but it can restart once the track is fixed. They come out for big wrecks, barrier repairs or weather.
explanation.incorrect: Red flags pause the race, not end it. Once the track is cleared and safe, the race restarts.

payload.prompt: A driver ignores a black flag. What happens?

options.text: No more laps are scored after that point.
They get a time penalty added to their finish.
They are automatically disqualified.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Ignoring the black flag means the race stops scoring their laps.
explanation.incorrect: When a driver ignores the black flag, NASCAR stops scoring their laps after a few laps of ignoring it, so they cannot finish in the results. Crews and drivers do not want that.

payload.prompt: What can bring out a yellow flag?
payload.template: A yellow flag is thrown for {{reasons}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Cautions protect everyone by slowing the field when something makes racing unsafe.
explanation.incorrect: Yellow flags come out when there's a crash, debris on track, or weather that makes racing dangerous.

lessons.title: Stages, explained
lessons.objective: Explain why races are split into stages and what stage points do.

payload.prompt: Why did NASCAR split races into stages?

options.text: To create multiple excitement moments and award points for each stage.
To make it harder for the leader to win.
To match football game halves.

explanation.correct: Yes. Stages create mini-races, so there are multiple climaxes and strategic decisions.
explanation.incorrect: Stages were added to create drama—each stage end is like a mini-finish with bonus points.

payload.prompt: Put the stage flow in order.

items.text: Stage one begins at green flag.
Top ten cars score stage points (10 down to 1).
Automatic caution at stage one's end.
Teams pit and adjust during the break.
Stage two restarts double file in the new running order.
Stage three runs until the race ends.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is how a race flows through stages, each with its own finish and pit window.
explanation.incorrect: Stages split a race into sections. The first two end with a planned caution and pit cycle, the last ends with the checkered flag, and the top ten score points at each stage end.

payload.prompt: How many stage points does the stage winner get?

options.text: 5 points
10 points
20 points

explanation.correct: Right. The stage winner gets 10; second gets 9, down to 1 for tenth.
explanation.incorrect: Stage points: 10 for first, 9 for second, and so on down to 1 for tenth place. Those add up.

payload.prompt: At a stage break, is it always better to pit for fresh tires?

scene.alt: Stage one ends at lap 60. The leader has old tires but leads by two seconds.

choices.label: No, some stay out for track position
Yes, fresh tires are always worth it.

explanation.correct: Exactly. If you lead, you might stay out to keep position, gambling old tires will hold.
explanation.incorrect: Track position can beat fresh tires. A leader might stay out at a stage break to keep the lead.

payload.prompt: Daytona 500, 200 laps, three stages. About how long is stage one?

explanation.correct: At Daytona, stage one is about 65 laps, roughly a third of the 200-lap race.
explanation.incorrect: Stage lengths are set per track and race, and NASCAR can adjust them. They roughly split the race into three parts, so about 65 laps at Daytona.

payload.prompt: When does the pace car come out at a stage break?

options.text: Immediately when the stage winner crosses the line.
After all cars finish and cross the line.
Only if there was a wreck during the stage.

explanation.correct: Right. The caution comes out automatically the moment the stage ends, with no wreck needed.
explanation.incorrect: The pace car comes out immediately when the stage winner crosses the line. It is a planned caution.

lessons.title: Cautions: why the race slows
lessons.objective: List why a caution is thrown and what happens next.

payload.prompt: Which does NOT cause a caution?

options.text: A car spins and debris is on track.
Heavy rain or lightning.
The leader is running a boring pit strategy.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Cautions are for safety. A slow pit strategy is never a reason, though stage breaks are planned cautions.
explanation.incorrect: Cautions are thrown for crashes, debris or weather, plus the planned stage-break cautions. A pit strategy alone never brings one out. Fans sometimes joke about debris nobody can see, but the stated reason is always safety.

payload.prompt: When a caution comes out, does the running order immediately change?

scene.alt: Yellow flag waves. First through fifth cars are on track in that order.

choices.label: No, the order freezes where everyone is
Yes, it re-sorts by pit strategy

explanation.correct: Exactly right. The running order locks in where cars are on track when yellow waves.
explanation.incorrect: When yellow flies, the running order freezes on track. Pit stops then reshuffle the field before the restart.

payload.prompt: Match the caution term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Leads the field at caution speed until the restart.
The window when most teams stop for fuel and tires.
A big lead evaporates because everyone resets to caution speed.
An automatic caution at the end of stages one and two.

distractorDefinitions: The driver who caused the caution.
A penalty for speeding on pit road.

explanation.summary: Cautions reset the race, bunch the field, and open pit windows.

payload.prompt: Can a caution actually help the second-place car?

options.text: No, cautions only help the leader by letting them rest.
Yes, it erases the leader's gap and gives second a fresh chance.
Cautions do not affect strategy at all.

explanation.correct: Absolutely. A caution wipes out a big lead and gives the trailing car a reset at restart.
explanation.incorrect: Cautions can flip the race. The leader's gap disappears, and the second-place car gets a fresh shot.

payload.prompt: Name the window when most teams stop under yellow.
payload.template: During a caution, teams usually pit during the {{time}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Under yellow, most of the field dives onto pit road in one wave, called the pit cycle.
explanation.incorrect: The pit cycle is the window when the majority of the field stops under caution for fuel and tires.

payload.prompt: Debris that could cut a tire is on the track. What happens?

options.text: A caution comes out so safety can remove it.
Drivers avoid it and racing continues.
The race is stopped permanently.

explanation.correct: Right. A loose piece of metal or rubber can cut a tire at racing speed, so officials throw a caution to clear it.
explanation.incorrect: Debris at racing speed is a hazard to every car behind it, so the field slows under caution while it is cleared. Racing does not just carry on.

lessons.title: Pit road, the basics
lessons.objective: Explain what happens on pit road and who is over the wall.

payload.prompt: Tap the spot where the fueler works.

diagram.alt: Overhead diagram of a pit stall with a car and five crew positions around it.

explanation.correct: Right. The fueler works at the car's fuel port on the pit-wall side, while the others handle the jack and tires.
explanation.incorrect: The fueler stands at the fuel port on the side of the car, away from the jack at the rear and the tire changers at the wheels.
explanation.sayThisLine: Their fueler got it in fast.

payload.prompt: Match the crew position to the job.

pairs.definition: Remove old tires and bolt on new ones.
Lifts the rear of the car off the ground.
Inserts the fuel nozzle into the fuel cell.
Hauls new tires from the stack to the changers.
The five specialists who jump the wall during a stop.

distractorDefinitions: Oversees the stop from the grandstand.

explanation.summary: Five crew members over the wall make pit stops possible: two tire changers, a jack man, a fueler, and a tire carrier.

payload.prompt: Why does NASCAR have a pit road speed limit?

options.text: To keep crew safe and prevent illegal speed advantages.
To make races longer.
Because pit road is too narrow.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Pit road is crowded with crew, so the speed limit protects everyone and keeps it fair.
explanation.incorrect: Pit road speed limits protect crew and prevent illegal advantages. Safety and fairness.

payload.prompt: If a driver speeds on pit road entry, what is the penalty?

scene.alt: Pit entry zone with speed check. Car is clocked at 52 mph when limit is 35 mph.

choices.label: Just a fine, no on-track penalty.

explanation.correct: Right. A drive-through means you pass through pit road at the limit without being serviced, then rejoin, so you lose the stop and track position.
explanation.incorrect: Speeding on pit road earns a drive-through penalty: you must go through pit road without service, which costs track position. It is not just a fine.

payload.prompt: Put the pit stop in order.

items.text: Driver enters pit road at legal speed.
Crew signals driver to their stall.
Car stops; crew jumps the wall.
Jack man lifts the car; changers remove old tires.
New tires bolt on; fueler connects.
Fueler disconnects; jack lowers car.
Driver leaves pit road and rejoins racing.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is the flow of a pit stop from entry to exit.
explanation.incorrect: A pit stop flows from entry to stop to service to exit. A clean four-tire stop takes roughly 10 to 12 seconds when it clicks.

payload.prompt: What is the main safety concern on pit road?

options.text: Five crew members working near a moving car with fuel and hazards.
Pit road is too short.
Drivers might fall asleep during stops.

explanation.correct: Absolutely. Crew is feet from a moving car, fuel is being transferred, and chaos is controlled.
explanation.incorrect: Pit road is one of the most dangerous places in racing—crew working by a car, fuel, flying tires.

lessons.title: Restarts and the choose rule
lessons.objective: Describe a restart and how the choose rule works.

payload.prompt: How are cars lined up at a restart?

options.text: Single file in running order.
Double file with leader and second place side by side.
Random order.

explanation.correct: Right. Double file with the leader and second place at the front, staggered.
explanation.incorrect: Restarts are double file. The leader and second place are side by side at the front.

payload.prompt: Tap the lane closest to the infield.

diagram.alt: Overhead of a double-file restart with two columns of cars; the inside column is closest to the infield.

explanation.correct: Right. Inside is the lane closest to the infield, on the driver's left. Under the choose rule, each driver picks inside or outside in running order.
explanation.incorrect: Inside means closest to the infield grass, on the left side of the field. The outside lane runs along the wall.

payload.prompt: Is the inside lane always the better choice at a restart?

scene.alt: Two lanes at a restart: which one is faster changes with the track, the tires and who is behind you.

choices.label: No, it depends on track type and moment

explanation.correct: Exactly. At some tracks the inside is quicker, at others the outside has the run, and it can change as the rubber builds up.
explanation.incorrect: Lane choice is strategy. Which lane has the run, the draft, or suits the track type? That is what drivers think about.

payload.prompt: Match the restart term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Getting a great start and launching past the next car.
Speed and momentum a trailing car builds in a lane.
Two-car-wide lineup with top two side by side.
Each driver picks inside or outside lane in running order.

distractorDefinitions: The speed limit on pit road.
The flashing lights on the pace car.

explanation.summary: Restarts reset the field and create passing opportunities. Timing, lane choice and momentum matter.

payload.prompt: Why do fans get excited about restarts?

options.text: Restarts bunch the field up and create big position swings.
The race is almost over.
Free tires are handed out.

explanation.correct: Right. Gaps are gone, cars are side by side and the green flag drops, so positions can change fast.
explanation.incorrect: Restarts are where gaps vanish and cars run side by side, so lots of passing happens there. Nobody hands out tires, and the race is not over.

payload.prompt: Complete the restart lineup rule.
payload.template: At a restart, the first car in line is the {{position}}, and they pick {{choice}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Under the choose rule the leader picks inside or outside first, then the rest choose in running order.
explanation.incorrect: The leader picks a lane first. Inside is the shorter way around; outside can get a run from the cars behind.

lessons.title: Overtime, red flags and finishing
lessons.objective: Explain overtime and why races run long.

payload.prompt: If a caution is thrown with one lap left, does the race go to overtime?

scene.alt: Three laps to go, yellow flag waves, race extends for green-white-checkered finish.

choices.label: Yes, extra laps for a green finish

explanation.correct: Yes. Overtime gives the race a chance to finish under green. Green-white-checkered.
explanation.incorrect: Overtime kicks in if a caution is near the end. The race extends for a green-flag finish.

payload.prompt: In green-white-checkered, what do the flags mean?

options.text: Green = restart, white = one lap to go, checkered = finish.
Green = leader winning, white = second place, checkered = third.
Green = pit stops allowed, white = no passing, checkered = stop.

explanation.correct: Right. Green restart, white for one final lap, checkered finishes the race.
explanation.incorrect: Green-white-checkered: restart on green, one lap warning on white, finish on checkered.

payload.prompt: Put the overtime sequence in order.

items.text: Yellow flag late in the race, around lap 198 of 200.
Race goes to overtime for a green-flag finish.
One last pit stop is allowed if teams choose.
Field lines up double file for restart.
Green flag waves—overtime restart.
White flag shows one lap remains.
Checkered flag ends the race.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is overtime: caution, reset, and one last lap under green.
explanation.incorrect: Overtime happens when caution is late. The race restarts, one lap runs, checkered ends it.

payload.prompt: When a red flag is thrown for weather, how long might it last?

options.text: Minutes for lightning, hours if a storm passes.
Always exactly 15 minutes.
Until the leader agrees to restart.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Lightning might clear in minutes, but a major storm can stop a race for hours.
explanation.incorrect: Red-flag duration depends on the cause. Lightning might clear quickly, but rain could stop a race for hours.

payload.prompt: A red flag {{reason}}, and {{action}} happens.

explanation.correct: Right. Red flag halts everything—all cars come to pit road and engines off.
explanation.incorrect: Red flags stop the race. All cars come to pit road. Engines off. Everyone waits.

payload.prompt: If a race is red-flagged late and never restarts due to weather, can it still have a winner?

scene.alt: Heavy storms approaching. Race stopped at lap 185 of 200. Weather will not clear.

choices.label: Yes, NASCAR declares the leader the win
No, the race must finish all laps.

explanation.correct: Yes. If the race is halted and cannot restart, NASCAR makes it official at that point.
explanation.incorrect: NASCAR can declare a race official even if it does not finish, as long as at least half the distance ran safely.

lessons.title: Lucky dogs and wave-arounds
lessons.objective: Explain how lapped cars return to the lead lap under caution.

payload.prompt: Match the lapped-car term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A car one or more full laps behind the leader; not in contention to win.
First lapped car gets to rejoin the lead lap without pitting under caution.
Lapped cars pass the pace car to unlap and rejoin the lead-lap group.
The group of cars on the leader's current lap; still able to win.

distractorDefinitions: A guaranteed caution for a lapped car.

explanation.summary: Free pass and wave-around are two ways lapped cars can get back in contention.

payload.prompt: Yellow flag just waved on lap 150 of 200. You are one lap down. What do you do?

situation.narrative: You are the first car one lap down, eligible for free pass.

facts.label: Your status
facts.value: One lap down, first in line for free pass.

facts.label: Free pass benefit
facts.value: You rejoin the lead lap without pitting.

facts.label: Restart position
facts.value: You will restart at the tail of the field.

options.label: Take the free pass
options.consequence: You rejoin the lead lap and are back in the race to win.

options.label: Pit anyway for fresh tires
options.consequence: You stay one lap down and lose the free pass opportunity.
considerations: You negate the free pass advantage
Fresh tires do not help if you are still lapped

options.label: Decline and stay on track
options.consequence: You stay one lap down and waste the free pass.
considerations: This is the prize for being first lapped car

payload.expertNote: Free pass is pure momentum—one lap for free and a reset. It is always taken.

payload.prompt: During a wave-around, which lapped cars can pass the pace car?

options.text: Only the first car one lap down.
All lapped cars can pass to rejoin the lead lap.
Only cars two or more laps down.

explanation.correct: Right. Wave-around is open to all lapped cars—they pass and rejoin.
explanation.incorrect: Wave-arounds let every lapped car pass the pace car and get back on the lead lap.

payload.prompt: Is a free pass the same as a wave-around?

scene.alt: Free pass: one car advances. Wave-around: multiple lapped cars pass pace car.

choices.label: No, free pass goes to one car
Yes, they are the same thing.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Free pass goes to the first lapped car; wave-around is for all lapped cars.
explanation.incorrect: Free pass is exclusive; wave-around is general. Different rules, same goal: get back on lead lap.

payload.prompt: Can a one-lap-down car still win the race?

options.text: No, lapped cars cannot win.
Yes, if they unlap and pass all lead-lap cars.
Only if the race leader crashes.

explanation.correct: Right. A lapped car can unlap and race back to the front.
explanation.incorrect: Being lapped is not a death sentence. If they unlap, they can race their way back.

payload.prompt: Under wave-around, lapped cars pass the {{location}} to rejoin the {{status}}.
payload.template: Under wave-around, lapped cars pass the {{location}} to rejoin the {{status}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Lapped cars pass the pace car and rejoin as lead-lap cars.
explanation.incorrect: Wave-around means lapped cars pass the pace car and rejoin the lead lap group.

lessons.title: A race in seven beats
lessons.objective: Narrate the shape and rhythm of a complete race from green to checkered.

payload.prompt: Put the major race moments in order.

items.text: Green flag drops and the field accelerates away.
Stage one finishes; top ten score stage points.
Caution at stage break; crews pit and adjust.
Field restarts in double file; passing happens.
Stage two finishes; another caution and pit cycle.
Stage three runs with incident cautions only.
Leader crosses first; checkered flag ends the race.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is the seven-beat shape: green, stage, restart, stage, restart, battle, checkered.
explanation.incorrect: A race flows in beats: start, stage, restart, stage, restart, battle, finish.

statement.speaker: Race fan
statement.text: They're pitting at the stage break now.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: The automatic caution just happened at stage end.
Top ten just finished stage points and are resetting strategy.
Pit road is closing and no one can pit anymore.

payload.translation: The automatic caution at stage end opened the pit window, so teams are servicing their cars.

followUps.line: What is the crew checking on this stop?
followUps.why: Shows you know pit crews make adjustments beyond fuel and tires.

followUps.line: Why might a team skip this pit stop?
followUps.why: Shows you understand track position strategy.

payload.title: Race day talk
payload.setting: A first-timer just watched a full race and wants to understand it.

exchanges.theirMessage: I have no idea what is going on with all these cautions and pit stops. What is the race actually doing?

replies.text: The race is split into three stages with pit stops between. That is the rhythm: go, caution, restart, repeat.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, so stages break it up. That makes sense.
replies.coachNote: You explained structure clearly without overloading.

replies.text: There are a lot of rules. Let me explain them all.
replies.theirResponse: But what is happening right now in the race?
replies.coachNote: He wants the story first, details later.

exchanges.theirMessage: So the stage is like a mini race?

replies.text: Exactly. Each stage has a finish line and the top ten score bonus points, then everyone resets.
replies.theirResponse: Got it. So three mini finishes plus the main finish.
replies.coachNote: You connected the dots. He gets it now.

replies.text: Kind of. But the real race is about pit strategy.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, but stages matter too, right?
replies.coachNote: True, but do not hedge. Stages are real mini-races.

exchanges.theirMessage: Why do they pit at every caution?

replies.text: They pit for fuel and fresh tires. Old tires fade, so new rubber helps them race and defend.
replies.coachNote: You explained the why, not just the what.

replies.text: Some teams pit and some stay out. Track position is the game.
replies.coachNote: Good, but explain what they are choosing between.

payload.closingNote: Races are a series of stages, cautions, restarts and strategy calls. The rhythm is the story.

payload.prompt: Why do races have three stages instead of one long race?

options.text: To create multiple climaxes and strategic decision points.
To make sure drivers do not get tired.
To give fans a scheduled race end time.

explanation.correct: Right. Stages create drama with multiple finish lines and pit cycles.
explanation.incorrect: Stages break the race into separate battles. Each has points and a strategic reset.

payload.prompt: Can an incident caution change the race flow significantly?

scene.alt: Stage two is running smoothly. An incident yellow waves early, changing pit cycles.

choices.label: Yes, it resets gaps and pit cycles
No, only stage breaks change strategy.

explanation.correct: Absolutely. Incident cautions are random and can flip everything.
explanation.incorrect: Incident cautions are chaos. They happen unexpectedly and reset pit cycles and running order.

payload.prompt: A race is finished when the {{condition}} {{milestone}}.
payload.template: A race is finished when the {{condition}} {{milestone}}.

options: crosses the finish on final lap
gaps.correct: crosses the finish on final lap

explanation.correct: Right. The first car to cross on the final lap wins and the checkered flag ends it.
explanation.incorrect: A race ends when the first car completes the full distance and crosses the finish line.
